title: The worst headache behind my left eye: recurrent unilateral headache with aura in a 32-year-old woman in general practice
desc: This station involves a focused headache history and a focused neurological examination of Sara, a 32-year-old accountant seen in general practice. She has a 14-hour throbbing left-sided headache that followed a visual and sensory aura, and she has had several similar attacks recently while under stress. The candidate then interprets her observations, a urine pregnancy test and her own headache record. They diagnose migraine with aura, make and explain an imaging decision, treat the current attack, stop the combined pill, and plan trigger management, smoking cessation, possible prevention and safety netting.
focus: Taking a structured headache history that screens for red flags, diagnosing migraine with aura, and recognising that the combined pill is contraindicated
diagnosis: Combined oral contraceptive contraindicated (migraine with aura)
Smoking and alcohol increased by stress
stem: You are a medical student on your general practice rotation. Sara, a 32-year-old accountant, has come in today with a headache. Your GP supervisor will see her after you.
tasks: Take a focused history from Sara and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Sara's observations, her urine pregnancy test and the headache record she has kept on her phone. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Sara, a 32-year-old accountant. You are in pain and you look it. You are wearing sunglasses and would like the lights dimmed. You speak quietly and slowly. You are worried and a little tearful when talking about how stressed you are. The examiner gives the examination findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: “I’ve got the worst headache. It started last night and it’s just getting worse.”

The headache (give only when asked):

  • Site: the left temple and behind the left eye. It does not spread anywhere else.
  • Onset: it started at about 8 pm last night, at home. It built up over an hour or two and has kept getting worse. It was not sudden, and it did not hit you like a blow to the head. It has now lasted about 14 hours. You barely slept.
  • Character: throbbing and pounding, in time with your heartbeat.
  • Severity: 10 out of 10.
  • What helps: lying in a dark, quiet room with an ice pack helps a little. Panadol helps slightly: you took 2 tablets at about 9 pm and 2 more at about 6 am.
  • What makes it worse: light, noise and moving around. It is not worse with coughing, straining or bending over.
  • Impact: “I can’t do anything.” You have called in sick to work today.

Before the headache (give only when asked what happened before it, about warning signs, or about changes in vision, numbness or tingling):

  • About an hour before the headache, at about 7 pm, your vision went “all spinny”. A shimmering, swirling patch of zigzag lights started near the middle of your vision and spread outwards over about 20 minutes, then faded. If asked: the room itself was not spinning, and you were not dizzy or off balance.
  • At about the same time you had tingling, then numbness, starting in your right hand and creeping up your right arm into the right side of your face and lips over 10 to 15 minutes. It had all gone completely within the hour, before the headache started.
  • No weakness, no trouble speaking or finding words, no facial droop and no loss of vision.

Other symptoms (give each only when asked):

  • Nausea: yes, since the headache started. You have not vomited.
  • Light and noise: both hurt. That is why you are wearing sunglasses.

Previous attacks (when asked whether this has happened before): “I’ve had several of these recently.” If asked how many: five, including this one, in the last two months, and you have been noting them in your phone. They are mostly on the left, but one was on the right. Some began with the same flashing, spinning vision and others did not; the one on the right also started with the zigzag lights. In the one on the right, the zigzag lights were on the left side of your vision and your left hand tingled. Each one lasted at least half a day, some more than a day. You never had headaches like these before the last couple of months. Between attacks you feel well.

Say no if asked about:

  • a sudden “thunderclap” headache, collapse or fainting;
  • fever, neck stiffness, a rash or feeling unwell beforehand;
  • being woken by the headache, headaches that are worst first thing in the morning, or headaches made worse by coughing or straining;
  • vomiting, weight loss, night sweats or feeling tired all the time;
  • a head injury;
  • jaw pain when chewing, a tender scalp or loss of vision;
  • a red or watering eye, a blocked or runny nose, or a droopy eyelid during the attacks;
  • restlessness or pacing during the pain (you want to lie completely still);
  • a tight band around your head;
  • recent travel or recent illness.

Past medical history: a dislocated shoulder at 15. Nothing else. No high blood pressure, clotting problems or previous stroke.

Medicines:

  • Panadol or Nurofen for the headaches. If asked how often: only on the days you have a headache, which is a day or two per attack.
  • “The pill.” Only if asked which kind, say: “The combined one, I think, with a week of sugar pills. I’ve been on it for years.” You have just kept taking it since the separation. Your last period was about 2 weeks ago and was normal.
  • Recreational drugs: you used marijuana in your 20s and none now.

Allergies: shellfish.

Family history: your mother has high blood pressure and has had migraines for as long as you can remember. Your father had prostate cancer. Your sister has asthma.

Social history:

  • Smoking: a social smoker, 2 or 3 cigarettes on weekends, but up to 5 a day when you are stressed, as you are now.
  • Alcohol: a glass of red wine on weeknights, more when stressed.
  • Work: an accountant. Work has been very busy with deadlines, and you wonder whether the workload is causing the headaches.
  • Activity and diet: Pilates on Saturdays. You meal prep but often buy lunch at a café.
  • Travel: none.
  • Home and supports: you recently separated from your partner and now live alone. Your family is interstate and you have only a few close friends. “I’m really stressed at the moment.”
  • Mood (only if asked): stressed and a bit lonely since the separation, but you do not feel depressed. You are sleeping badly when work is busy. You have no thoughts of harming yourself.

Ideas, concerns and expectations:

  • Idea: you wonder whether it is the stress and the workload.
  • Concern (say this when asked what worries you): “I’m scared it’s a brain tumour. And the stress just makes it all worse.”
  • Expectation: you want something to stop the pain and to stop these attacks.

Question to raise near the end of Part 1: “Do I need a brain scan?” Accept a brief answer, or a promise to come back to it once the results are back.

Exam findings (examiner: give only when the candidate says what they are examining):

  • General inspection: alert and oriented. Uncomfortable, sitting still with sunglasses on and asking for the lights to be dimmed. Not pale or flushed. No rash.
  • Observations: the practice nurse has done them. Temperature 36.8 °C, BP 122/78 mmHg, HR 84/min regular, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, capillary glucose 5.6 mmol/L. (The full set is handed over in Part 2.)
  • Meningism: no neck stiffness. Kernig’s sign negative. Brudzinski negative (if tested).
  • Fundoscopy: optic discs pink with sharp margins and no swelling. Spontaneous venous pulsations present. No haemorrhages.
  • Eyes: visual acuity 6/6 in each eye. Visual fields full to confrontation. Pupils equal, round and reactive to light, with no relative afferent pupillary defect. No ptosis or miosis. Eye movements full, with no nystagmus or double vision. No conjunctival redness or tearing.
  • Other cranial nerves: facial sensation and movement normal and symmetrical. Palate, tongue and shoulder shrug normal. No rhinorrhoea.
  • Limbs: no pronator drift. Tone, power (5/5), reflexes and sensation (light touch and pinprick) normal and symmetrical in all four limbs, including the hands. Plantars flexor.
  • Coordination and gait: finger-nose and heel-shin normal. Gait normal, including heel-to-toe walking. Romberg negative.
  • Head and neck: temporal arteries palpable, pulsatile and non-tender. No scalp tenderness. Sinuses non-tender. No tenderness of the neck or shoulder muscles. Neck movements full.
  • Mental state (if commented on): appropriately dressed, cooperative and anxious. Speech normal but quiet. Mood “stressed”, with an anxious affect. No thoughts of self-harm.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Sara's identity, explains the examination and gains consent; offers to dim the lights given her photophobia.
Empathic and non-judgemental: acknowledges her pain and her fear of a brain tumour, asks about smoking, alcohol and drugs without judgement, and uses plain language.
History
Characterises the headache:

kids.x: Site: left temple and behind the left eye (unilateral), with no radiation.
Onset and time course: began about 8 pm last night and built up over hours (not sudden or thunderclap); has lasted 14 hours and is getting worse.
kids.d: Award only if the speed of onset is specifically asked about.

kids.x: Character and severity: throbbing, 10/10.
Relieving and aggravating factors: a dark quiet room, ice packs and Panadol help slightly; worse with light, noise and movement, not with coughing or straining.
Pattern: five similar attacks in 2 months, mostly on the left and once on the right; well between attacks; no headaches like these before.

check.x: Asks about symptoms before the headache and finds the aura: a shimmering, spinning zigzag patch spreading over about 20 minutes, with tingling then numbness spreading from the right hand into the right side of the face, all fully resolved within the hour before the headache began; no weakness, speech disturbance or loss of vision.
check.d: Award only if the candidate establishes that the symptoms spread gradually and resolved completely.

check.x: Asks about associated symptoms: nausea without vomiting, photophobia and phonophobia.
Asks about the impact on daily life: cannot do anything, off work today.
Screens for red flags of a secondary headache:

kids.x: Subarachnoid haemorrhage: sudden thunderclap onset peaking within a minute, collapse [no].
Meningitis: fever, neck stiffness, rash [no].
Raised intracranial pressure or tumour: wakes her from sleep, worse in the morning or with coughing or straining, vomiting, weight loss or night sweats [no].
Head injury and persisting focal symptoms (weakness, speech, facial droop, visual loss) [no].
Pattern: establishes that the headaches are new in the last 2 months (no previous similar headaches).

check.x: Asks about features of other headache types: cluster (red watering eye, runny nose, droopy eyelid, restlessness), tension-type (tight band, both sides) and temporal arteritis (jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, visual loss) [all absent].
check.d: Award if features of at least two of these are asked about.

check.x: Takes the past medical history and allergies: dislocated shoulder at 15; no hypertension, clotting problems or previous stroke; allergic to shellfish.
Takes a medication and drug history:

kids.x: Identifies that she takes the combined oral contraceptive pill (asks which type).
kids.d: Award only if the candidate establishes that the pill is the combined (oestrogen-containing) type.

kids.x: Quantifies analgesic use: Panadol or Nurofen only on headache days, a day or two per attack.
Asks about recreational drugs: marijuana in her 20s, none now.

check.x: Takes a family history: mother has long-standing migraines and hypertension; father had prostate cancer; sister has asthma.
Takes a social history:

kids.x: Smoking, quantified: 2 or 3 cigarettes on weekends, up to 5 a day when stressed.
Alcohol, quantified: a glass of red wine on weeknights, more when stressed.
Work, home and supports: accountant under deadline pressure, recently separated, lives alone, family interstate, few close friends; Pilates on Saturdays; no recent travel.

check.x: Screens mood, sleep and safety: stressed and sleeping poorly, not depressed, no thoughts of self-harm.
Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: wonders whether it is work stress, fears a brain tumour, wants the pain and the attacks to stop.
Examination
Asks for the observations, including blood pressure and temperature [BP 122/78, temperature 36.8 °C, all normal].
General inspection: distress, photophobia, rash [uncomfortable, photophobic, no rash].
Examines for meningism: neck stiffness and Kernig's sign [negative].
Performs fundoscopy to look for papilloedema [sharp discs, spontaneous venous pulsations present].

Examines the eyes and cranial nerves: acuity, visual fields, pupils (including ptosis and miosis), eye movements, facial sensation and movement [all normal, no Horner syndrome, no red or watering eye].
Examines the limbs for a focal deficit: pronator drift, tone, power, reflexes, sensation and plantars [all normal].
Assesses coordination and gait, including heel-to-toe walking [normal].
Palpates the temporal arteries and scalp, and checks the sinuses and neck muscles [non-tender, pulsatile temporal arteries].
Interpretation
Interprets the observations as normal: afebrile, normotensive on repeat, normal glucose, so no sign of infection, hypertensive headache or hypoglycaemia, and her BP allows a triptan.
Interprets the negative urine pregnancy test: she is not pregnant, so medicines can be prescribed and her contraception changed safely.

Interprets the headache record: 5 attacks in 8 weeks (about 2 to 3 a month), each 12 to 36 hours, aura before 3 of them, including the one right-sided attack; analgesics on about 7 to 8 days in 8 weeks, so no medication-overuse headache; triggers of stress, alcohol and poor sleep; disabling enough (3 days off work) to discuss prevention.
check.d: Award if frequency, analgesic days and at least one trigger are all interpreted.

check.x: Gives migraine with aura as the most likely diagnosis, justified by a unilateral, pulsating, disabling headache lasting hours with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia, preceded by a gradually spreading, fully reversible visual and sensory aura, with a family history and a normal examination.
Names differentials, each with a feature for or against from this case: tension-type headache, cluster headache, temporal arteritis, TIA, subarachnoid haemorrhage.
check.d: Award for at least three, including TIA, each justified. Also credit cerebral venous sinus thrombosis if offered and justified.

check.x: Makes a justified imaging decision: no urgent imaging (no CT for reassurance), recognising both the reassuring features (typical ICHD-3 aura, side varies, well between attacks, normal examination including fundi) and the flags (headaches new in the last 2 months, first aura on the combined pill). Either concludes imaging is not needed now with clear triggers for imaging (aura over 60 minutes, motor weakness, always the same side, progression, new signs), or proposes a non-urgent MRI after discussion with the supervisor.
check.d: Do not award for an unjustified CT for reassurance, or for no scan without acknowledging the new-onset pattern.

check.x: Management
Explains migraine with aura in plain language and reassures her honestly that the history and examination do not suggest a tumour.
Treats the current attack:

kids.x: Gives an appropriate acute regimen for this attack: soluble aspirin 900 mg or an NSAID (e.g. ibuprofen 400 mg) with metoclopramide 10 mg orally, OR a triptan (e.g. sumatriptan 50 to 100 mg orally) with or without an antiemetic; avoids opioids including codeine.
kids.d: Accept either pathway without exact doses; do not award if an opioid is given.

kids.x: Explains timing of acute treatment: take it early in the headache phase; if a triptan is used (now or for future attacks), take it once the headache has started, not during the aura.
kids.d: Award for advice to treat early in the headache; the triptan-timing point is required only if a triptan is offered.

check.x: Addresses contraception:

kids.x: Stops the combined pill and explains that oestrogen-containing contraception is contraindicated in migraine with aura because it increases the risk of stroke, which smoking increases further.
Offers alternatives: a progestogen-only method (implant, hormonal IUD, progestogen-only pill or injection) or a copper IUD, with condoms in the meantime if needed.

check.x: Advises on triggers and lifestyle: keep a headache diary, regular sleep and meals, limit alcohol, stress management.
Gives brief smoking cessation advice and offers Quitline (13 7848) and support to quit.

Discusses preventive treatment because attacks are frequent and disabling (for example propranolol, amitriptyline or candesartan; candesartan is contraindicated in pregnancy, so use it only with reliable contraception), and advises limiting acute medicines to avoid medication-overuse headache.
check.d: Award for naming one preventive option and the overuse limit.

check.x: Offers support for stress: a GP mental health treatment plan with a psychologist, or her employee assistance program, and a medical certificate for work today.
Safety netting

Names red flags in plain words: call 000 immediately for any weakness, face drooping or trouble speaking (these are not part of her aura), or for numbness or visual symptoms that come on suddenly, last more than an hour or are different from her usual aura; also a sudden severe headache that peaks within a minute, fever with a stiff neck or rash, confusion or a seizure.
check.d: Award for a sudden severe headache plus at least one stroke symptom with immediate 000.

check.x: Advises same-day review (GP or ED) if this attack does not settle with the treatment, has lasted more than 72 hours, or she cannot keep fluids down.
Arranges follow-up: GP review in about 4 weeks with the headache diary (to judge treatment and prevention), a contraception appointment, and written information.

part2.lead: Here are Sara's observations from the practice nurse, the urine pregnancy test the nurse did before you saw her, and the headache record Sara has kept on her phone over the last 8 weeks.
part2.patient:
• When the candidate explains the diagnosis, ask: “So it’s not a tumour? Shouldn’t I have a scan just to be sure?” Settle if the candidate explains clearly why a scan is not needed now and what would change that, or explains why a non-urgent MRI is reasonable.
  • When the pill comes up: “But I’ve been on that pill for years. Why do I have to stop it now? What do I use instead?”
  • If smoking is raised: “It’s only a few. I only really smoke when I’m stressed.” Agree to think about Quitline if it is offered kindly.

handover.label: Observations (practice nurse, today)
handover.result: Taken in a dimmed treatment room; repeat BP after 10 minutes' rest.
handover.model:
• Read: RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, HR 84 then 80 and regular, BP 122/78 then 124/76 mmHg, temperature 36.8 °C, alert, capillary glucose 5.6 mmol/L. Pain 10/10. Every value is within normal adult ranges (it would sit in the white zone of an adult observation chart), so no escalation is needed.
  • For Sara: afebrile, so no sign of meningitis or another infection. Normotensive, so not a hypertensive headache. Normal glucose. Her vital signs are stable despite severe pain.
  • What it changes: she can be managed in general practice. A normal BP means there is no contraindication to a triptan. It is also a baseline for propranolol or candesartan if prevention is started (candesartan is contraindicated in pregnancy, so use it only with reliable contraception).

rows.note: Seated in a dimmed room, sunglasses on

handover.label: Urine pregnancy test (point of care, today)
handover.result: Point-of-care urine hCG, tested by the practice nurse at 10:10. Last menstrual period about 2 weeks ago.
handover.model:
• Read: urine hCG negative, with a normal period 2 weeks ago.
  • For Sara: she is not pregnant, so a pregnancy-related cause of headache does not arise, and NSAIDs, a triptan and preventive medicines can be prescribed.
  • What it changes: it is safe to stop the combined pill today and start a progestogen-only method or arrange an IUD, using condoms in the meantime if she is sexually active.

handover.model:
• Read: 5 discrete attacks in 8 weeks (about 2 to 3 a month), each lasting 12 to 36 hours and severe, with an aura before 3, including the one right-sided attack. She was headache-free between attacks. She took acute medicines on about 7 to 8 days in 8 weeks.
  • For Sara: recurrent stereotyped attacks lasting 12 to 36 hours (within 4 to 72 hours) fit migraine with aura (at least 2 attacks with typical aura), with some attacks occurring without aura, which is common. Aura and headache arise from either side, which is reassuring against a fixed structural lesion. Analgesics are used on well under 15 days a month, so this is not medication-overuse headache. The triggers are clear: work deadlines, alcohol, poor sleep and skipped meals.
  • What it changes: attacks this frequent and disabling (3 days off work) justify discussing a preventive medicine as well as trigger management. The record becomes the baseline for judging the response, and she should keep it going.

ask: You are now handing over to your GP supervisor. Please give an ISBAR handover of Sara, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Sara now, here in general practice.
Before Sara goes home, what would you tell her and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: medical student; Sara, 32, accountant.
  • Situation: 14-hour throbbing left temporal and retro-orbital headache, 10/10, after a visual and sensory aura that resolved within an hour; nausea, photophobia, phonophobia; fears a tumour.
  • Background: five similar attacks in 2 months; mother has migraines; takes the combined pill; smokes up to 5 a day and drinks more when stressed; recently separated, lives alone.
  • Assessment: headaches new in the last 2 months and first aura on the combined pill, but the aura is typical and there are no other red flags; no meningism, normal fundi and normal neurological examination. Observations normal. Urine hCG negative. Diary: about 2 to 3 attacks a month, analgesics on about 7 to 8 days, no overuse, stress and alcohol triggers. Migraine with aura.
  • Recommendation: treat the attack now (NSAID plus antiemetic or a triptan); stop the combined pill and offer a progestogen-only or copper method; discuss prevention and smoking; review in 4 weeks.

Most likely: migraine with aura. For: unilateral, pulsating, disabling headache lasting hours, with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia (POUND); preceded by a gradually spreading, fully reversible visual and sensory aura; recurrent stereotyped attacks; family history; normal examination.

  • Tension-type headache: against: one-sided, throbbing, severe, with aura and nausea.
  • Cluster headache: against: attacks last 12 to 36 hours, not 15 to 180 minutes; no tearing, red eye or restlessness.
  • TIA: for: transient sensory symptoms on the pill and smoking. Against: positive symptoms spreading gradually, then headache.
  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage: against: gradual onset over hours, no meningism.
  • Also credit: temporal arteritis: against: aged 32 with normal temporal arteries.
  • Also credit: cerebral venous sinus thrombosis: against: discrete attacks with full recovery and normal fundi.

Imaging: no urgent scan; justify (see item 32).

1. Treat this attack: soluble aspirin 900 mg or ibuprofen 400 mg with metoclopramide 10 mg orally; or sumatriptan 50 to 100 mg once the headache has started (not during the aura). Avoid opioids.
  2. Contraception: stop the combined pill (oestrogen is contraindicated with aura: stroke risk); offer an implant, hormonal or copper IUD, or a progestogen-only pill; condoms in the meantime.
  3. Prevention: offer propranolol, amitriptyline or candesartan; limit acute medicines to avoid overuse.
  4. Triggers and smoking: regular sleep and meals, less alcohol; brief smoking advice, Quitline 13 7848.

• Call 000 immediately: any weakness, face drooping or trouble speaking (these are not part of her aura), or numbness or visual symptoms that come on suddenly, last more than an hour or are different from her usual aura; also a sudden severe headache that peaks within a minute, fever with a stiff neck or rash, confusion or a seizure.
  • Same day (GP or ED): this attack not settling with treatment or lasting more than 72 hours, or vomiting so she cannot keep fluids or tablets down.
  • Medicines: take treatment early in the headache; use acute medicines on fewer than 10 days a month.
  • Triggers: regular sleep and meals, less alcohol.
  • Follow-up: GP review in about 4 weeks with the diary; contraception appointment; smoking support; stress support (GP mental health plan with a psychologist, or employee assistance program); written information; a medical certificate for today.

ddx.for: A unilateral, throbbing, disabling headache lasting hours with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia, preceded by a gradually spreading, fully reversible visual and sensory aura; recurrent stereotyped attacks; mother has migraines; normal examination.
Headaches have come with work stress and poor sleep.
ddx.against: Her headache is one-sided, throbbing and severe, with aura, nausea, photophobia and phonophobia, and is worse with movement.

ddx.for: Severe one-sided pain around the eye, and she smokes and drinks alcohol.
ddx.against: Attacks last 12 to 36 hours rather than 15 to 180 minutes, with no tearing, red eye, runny nose or ptosis, and she lies still rather than pacing.

ddx.for: Transient numbness of the right hand and face in a woman on the combined pill who smokes.
ddx.against: The symptoms were positive (lights, tingling), spread gradually over minutes, resolved fully and were followed by a typical migraine headache, and her examination is normal.

ddx.for: A severe headache she rates 10 out of 10.
ddx.against: The headache built up over hours rather than peaking within a minute, follows a pattern of similar attacks, and she has no meningism or focal signs.

ddx.for: New headaches in the last 2 months in a woman on combined oestrogen who smokes.
ddx.against: Discrete attacks with complete recovery in between, a typical aura, normal fundi with spontaneous venous pulsations and no persisting deficit.

guide:
In Part 1 give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. Sara gives the aura only when asked what happened before the headache, about warning signs, or about changes in vision, numbness or tingling. She says “several” attacks until asked how many. She calls her medicine “the pill” and says it is the combined type only if asked which kind. Her “spinning vision” is a visual aura, not vertigo: if asked, the room was not spinning. The history should take about 6 minutes, leaving time for meningism, fundoscopy and a screening neurological examination. Accept a stated, briefly described examination. The observations are given as values in Part 1, and the full set is handed over in Part 2.

In Part 2 hand over all three results together and ask the four questions in order. Sara asks about a scan and the pill while the candidate explains. Score item 34 from the diagnosis answer or the response to Sara's scan question. Score items 35 and 36 from the management answer. Credit items 34, 37, 38 and 39 from the management, diagnosis or follow-up answer, wherever they are given. Score item 40 from the follow-up answer. Score the safety-netting items from the fourth question. Credit item 32 (imaging decision) whether it is given in the diagnosis or the management answer, or in reply to Sara's scan question. If the type of pill was not established in Part 1, item 12.1 cannot be awarded, but item 36 can still be earned in Part 2 once the candidate asks about her contraception.

A high-performing candidate characterises the headache systematically and establishes the gradual onset. They draw out an aura that spreads and resolves fully, and cluster their red flag questions by differential (SAH, meningitis, raised pressure, stroke, temporal arteritis, cluster). They find the combined pill, the smoking and the stress. They examine for meningism, papilloedema and focal signs. In Part 2 they use the diary to judge frequency and exclude medication overuse, diagnose migraine with aura, and make and explain an honest imaging decision. They treat the attack with an NSAID and antiemetic or a triptan, stop the combined pill because of stroke risk and offer alternatives, and give clear red flags.

A borderline candidate takes a generic pain history, misses the aura or the speed of onset, or never asks which pill she takes. They skip fundoscopy and meningism, order an urgent CT “to reassure her” without justification, prescribe codeine, or leave her on the combined pill. Their safety netting is vague (“come back if it gets worse”).
explain:
Approach to headache

The first job is to separate a primary headache (migraine, tension-type, cluster) from a secondary headache that signals another disease. Cluster your questions by diagnosis:

  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage: a thunderclap headache that peaks within a minute, often with collapse or vomiting.
  • Meningitis: fever, neck stiffness, rash, photophobia, drowsiness.
  • Raised intracranial pressure or tumour: headache that wakes the patient or is worst on waking, worse with coughing or straining, vomiting, new neurological signs, weight loss or a cancer history.
  • Stroke or TIA: sudden negative symptoms (weakness, numbness, speech loss, visual loss), more likely in older people with vascular risk factors.
  • Temporal arteritis: new headache over 50, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, visual symptoms.
  • Pattern: a new or recently changed headache pattern, and a first aura while on combined hormonal contraception.
  • Others: head injury, pregnancy and the postpartum period, immunosuppression, medication overuse.

Risk stratification matters. Migraine is most common in young women with a family history, whereas stroke and temporal arteritis are diseases of older people. Ask how the headache affects daily life, and assess mood and supports, particularly when stress is a trigger.

Why Sara has migraine with aura

The POUND mnemonic summarises the migraine headache: Pulsatile, hOurs (4 to 72), Unilateral, Nausea, Disabling. Sara has every feature, plus photophobia and phonophobia. ICHD-3 defines an aura as fully reversible visual, sensory or speech symptoms, with at least three of the following:

  • at least one symptom spreads gradually over 5 minutes or more;
  • two or more symptoms occur in succession;
  • each symptom lasts 5 to 60 minutes;
  • at least one symptom is unilateral;
  • at least one symptom is positive (lights, tingling);
  • headache accompanies the aura or follows it within 60 minutes.

Her shimmering zigzag lights spreading over 20 minutes, then tingling followed by numbness spreading from her right hand into the right side of her face, all resolved and followed by the headache, meet these criteria. Her risk factors are female sex, a mother with migraine, stress, alcohol and poor sleep. Smoking and the combined pill add to her vascular risk.

Differentials

  • TIA: the key distinction is the quality and tempo of the symptoms. TIA symptoms are typically sudden, negative and maximal at onset. A migrainous aura is positive, spreads gradually and is followed by headache. An aura that lasts more than an hour, is purely negative, or is new or different in an older person with vascular risk needs urgent assessment.
  • Tension-type headache: bilateral, pressing, mild to moderate, without nausea or aura.
  • Cluster headache: strictly one-sided orbital pain lasting 15 to 180 minutes, with tearing, a red eye, rhinorrhoea or ptosis and restlessness. It is more common in men who smoke.
  • Temporal arteritis: almost never under 50.
  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage and meningitis: excluded clinically by the gradual onset, the normal temperature and the absence of meningism.
  • Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis: worth considering with new headaches in a woman taking combined oestrogen who smokes, but her discrete attacks with complete recovery between them, typical aura, normal fundi with spontaneous venous pulsations and lack of any persisting deficit are against it.

The results

Her observations are normal. The urine pregnancy test is negative, so treatment and a change of contraception are safe. Her own record shows 5 attacks in 8 weeks with aura before 3, including the one right-sided attack, whose aura came from the other side (left visual field, left hand), so aura and headache arise from either side, which is reassuring against a fixed structural lesion. Analgesics were used on about 7 to 8 days, so there is no medication-overuse headache (simple analgesics on 15 or more days a month, or triptans or combination analgesics on 10 or more days a month, for more than 3 months). Her triggers are clear. Her headaches are recent in onset and her first aura came while on the combined pill, which call for careful assessment, but they do not mandate imaging here because the aura meets ICHD-3 criteria, the side varies, she is well between attacks and her examination, including fundoscopy, is normal; imaging would be needed if the aura became atypical (over 60 minutes, motor weakness, always the same side), the pattern progressed or new signs developed. Some guidance lists a first aura on combined hormonal contraception as an indication to consider referral or imaging; stopping the oestrogen and reviewing early is the safe response here, and discussing imaging with the supervisor is reasonable. With a typical history and a normal examination, neuroimaging is not indicated now, and scanning “for reassurance” often finds incidental findings that cause more anxiety.

Management (eTG Neurology)

  • Acute attacks: treat early in the headache. Use soluble aspirin 900 mg or an NSAID such as ibuprofen 400 mg, or paracetamol 1 g, with an antiemetic such as metoclopramide 10 mg orally, which also improves absorption. If that fails, use a triptan such as sumatriptan 50 to 100 mg orally, taken when the headache begins rather than during the aura. A dose can be repeated after 2 hours if the headache returns. Avoid opioids, including codeine: they work poorly and promote medication overuse. If she is vomiting, a parenteral antiemetic is needed, and if the attack does not settle she should go to ED.
  • Contraception: combined (oestrogen-containing) hormonal contraception is contraindicated at any age in migraine with aura (UKMEC category 4) because it increases the risk of ischaemic stroke. Smoking adds to that risk. Stop the combined pill and offer a progestogen-only method (implant, hormonal IUD, progestogen-only pill or injection) or a copper IUD.
  • Triggers and lifestyle: a headache diary, regular sleep and meals, less alcohol, regular exercise and stress management. Offer a GP mental health treatment plan for psychology, given the separation, living alone and limited supports.
  • Smoking: brief advice using Ask, Advise, Help, referral to Quitline (13 7848) and pharmacotherapy.
  • Prevention: consider a preventive medicine when attacks are frequent or disabling, or acute treatment fails. Options include propranolol, amitriptyline, candesartan and pizotifen. Candesartan is contraindicated in pregnancy, so use it only with reliable contraception. Topiramate is teratogenic and reduces the effectiveness of hormonal contraception, so it needs care in a woman of reproductive age. Give each preventive a trial of 2 to 3 months, judged against the diary.

Safety netting

Sara should call 000 immediately for any weakness, face drooping or trouble speaking (these are not part of her aura), or for numbness or visual symptoms that come on suddenly, last more than an hour or are different from her usual aura; also for a sudden severe headache that peaks within a minute, fever with a stiff neck or rash, confusion or a seizure. She should seek same-day review if this attack does not settle, lasts more than 72 hours, or she cannot keep fluids down. Review in about 4 weeks with her diary, with a contraception appointment and support for smoking and stress.

A triptan dose may be repeated after 2 hours if the headache returns, and the other acute option can be used if the first fails.
points: Separate primary from secondary headache by clustering your questions by diagnosis: SAH (thunderclap onset), meningitis (fever, stiff neck, rash), raised pressure (waking, worse with coughing or straining, vomiting), stroke or TIA, and temporal arteritis (over 50).

POUND (Pulsatile, hOurs 4 to 72, Unilateral, Nausea, Disabling) supports migraine. A positive aura that spreads over minutes and resolves fully within an hour before the headache marks migraine with aura.
A migrainous aura is positive and spreads gradually, whereas a TIA is sudden, negative and maximal at onset. An aura that lasts more than an hour or is unlike the usual one needs urgent assessment.

Combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated in migraine with aura because of the increased risk of stroke, and smoking adds to it. Always ask which pill a woman with migraine takes, and offer a progestogen-only or copper method.
Treat attacks early with aspirin or an NSAID plus an antiemetic, or a triptan once the headache starts. Avoid opioids, and keep acute medicine days low to prevent medication-overuse headache.
A typical history with a normal examination, including fundoscopy and meningism, needs no brain imaging. A headache diary guides the decision to start prevention and shows whether it works.
